title: Static Electricity and Charge: Conservation of Charge
lead: Rubbing amber with silk has been known to make it attract straw since the ancient Greeks noticed it, and the quantity that explains what rubbing does is electric charge. This section says what charge is and why there are two types of it, how electrons and protons carry it in one basic amount that every observed charge is a whole number of, how many of them make a coulomb, and why rubbing separates charge rather than creating it, closing on the law that the total charge of any process never changes, even where a pair of particles is made out of energy.
objectives: Define electric charge, and describe how the two types of charge interact.
Describe three common situations that generate static electricity.
State the law of conservation of charge.
summary_html:
• There are only two types of charge, which we call positive and negative.
  • Like charges repel, unlike charges attract, and the force between charges decreases with the square of the distance.
  • The vast majority of positive charge in nature is carried by protons, while the vast majority of negative charge is carried by electrons.
  • The electric charge of one electron is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the charge of one proton.
  • An ion is an atom or molecule that has nonzero total charge due to having unequal numbers of electrons and protons.
  • The SI unit for charge is the coulomb (C), with protons and electrons having charges of opposite sign but equal magnitude; the magnitude of this basic charge $|\kqe|$ is $|\kqe| = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$.
  • Whenever charge is created or destroyed, equal amounts of positive and negative are involved.
  • Most often, existing charges are separated from neutral objects to obtain some net charge.
  • Both positive and negative charges exist in neutral objects and can be separated by rubbing one object with another. For macroscopic objects, negatively charged means an excess of electrons and positively charged means a depletion of electrons.
  • The law of conservation of charge ensures that whenever a charge is created, an equal charge of the opposite sign is created at the same time.
notes: The PhET simulation Balloons and Static Electricity is left out, as are the two problems the book leaves unkeyed, the electrons moved through a pocket calculator in a day and the fundamental units of charge in a lightning bolt.

When materials are rubbed together, charges can be separated, particularly if one material has a greater affinity for electrons than another. (a) Both the amber and cloth are originally neutral, with equal positive and negative charges. Only a tiny fraction of the charges are involved, and only a few of them are shown here. (b) When rubbed together, some negative charge is transferred to the amber, leaving the cloth with a net positive charge. (c) When separated, the amber and cloth now have net charges, but the absolute value of the net positive and negative charges will be equal.

(a) When enough energy is present, it can be converted into matter. Here the matter created is an electron–antielectron pair. (m_e is the electron’s mass.) The total charge before and after this event is zero. (b) When matter and antimatter collide, they annihilate each other; the total charge is conserved at zero before and after the annihilation.

exercises.prompt: There are very large numbers of charged particles in most objects. Why, then, don’t most objects exhibit static electricity?

answer.solution: Because the charges in an ordinary object come in two types that cancel. Every atom holds as many electrons as protons, and the charge of an electron is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the charge of a proton, so the enormous numbers of positive and negative charges in a piece of matter add to nothing. What an object shows to the world is its net charge, and that is the small difference between two huge numbers, not the numbers themselves. Static electricity appears only when something, usually rubbing, moves a tiny fraction of the electrons from one object to another and leaves the two with a net charge of opposite sign.

exercises.prompt: Why do most objects tend to contain nearly equal numbers of positive and negative charges?

answer.solution: Because unlike charges attract. An object that had many more protons than electrons would pull electrons toward it from everything around it, and one with too many electrons would give them up just as readily, until the numbers were nearly equal again. The attraction between the two types of charge is very strong, so a large imbalance cannot be kept: matter settles into atoms with as many electrons as protons, and the objects built out of those atoms are neutral to a very good approximation. The charge that rubbing separates is a tiny fraction of what an object holds.

exercises.prompt:
When a glass rod is rubbed against silk, which of the following statements is true?
  1. Electrons are removed from the silk.
  2. Electrons are removed from the rod.
  3. Protons are removed from the silk.
  4. Protons are removed from the rod.

options: Electrons are removed from the silk.
Electrons are removed from the rod.
Protons are removed from the silk.
Protons are removed from the rod.
answer.hint: Rubbing moves electrons, never protons, and the glass ends up positively charged.

exercises.prompt:
In an experiment, three microscopic latex spheres are sprayed into a chamber and become charged with +3e, +5e, and −3e, respectively. Later, all three spheres collide simultaneously and then separate. Which of the following are possible values for the final charges on the spheres? Select two answers.
XYZ
(a)+4e−4e+5e
(b)−4e+4.5e+5.5e
(c)+5e−8e+7e
(d)+6e+6e−7e

answer.solution: Two conditions have to hold at once. The law of conservation of charge says the three final charges must add to the total the spheres started with, which is $+3e + 5e - 3e = +5e$, and the elementary charge says every charge must be a whole number of $e$, since all observed charges are integral multiples of the basic charge. Add up each row and look for a fraction. Row (a) comes to $+5e$ and is whole throughout. Row (b) comes to $+6e$ and carries halves of $e$, so it fails both tests. Row (c) comes to $+4e$, which is not the charge the spheres began with. Row (d) comes to $+5e$ and is whole throughout. The two possible sets are therefore (a) and (d).

exercises.prompt:
If objects X and Y attract each other, which of the following will be false?
  1. X has positive charge and Y has negative charge.
  2. X has negative charge and Y has positive charge.
  3. X and Y both have positive charge.
  4. X is neutral and Y has a charge.

options: X has positive charge and Y has negative charge.
X has negative charge and Y has positive charge.
X and Y both have positive charge.
X is neutral and Y has a charge.
answer.hint: Like charges repel. Ask which of the four situations is the only one in which the two objects carry the same sign.

exercises.prompt:
Suppose a positively charged object A is brought in contact with an uncharged object B in a closed system. What type of charge will be left on object B?
  1. negative
  2. positive
  3. neutral
  4. cannot be determined

answer.solution: The system is closed, so the total charge cannot change: whatever B gains, A loses. A is positively charged, which means it is short of electrons, so when the two touch, electrons pass from B to A. B is left short of electrons in its turn, and a shortage of electrons is a positive charge. So B ends up positively charged, which is option (b), and the two positive charges together still add to the charge A started with.

exercises.prompt:
What will be the net charge on an object which attracts neutral pieces of paper but repels a negatively charged balloon?
  1. negative
  2. positive
  3. neutral
  4. cannot be determined

answer.hint: Repulsion is the telling observation: only like charges repel, and a neutral object attracts either sign.

exercises.prompt:
When two neutral objects are rubbed against each other, the first one gains a net charge of 3e. Which of the following statements is true?
  1. The second object gains 3e and is negatively charged.
  2. The second object loses 3e and is negatively charged.
  3. The second object gains 3e and is positively charged.
  4. The second object loses 3e and is positively charged.

answer.solution: Both objects were neutral to begin with, so the total charge is zero before the rubbing and must still be zero after it. If the first object has a net charge of $+3e$, the second must carry $-3e$, and a negative charge is an excess of electrons. The first object lost three electrons to the second, so the second gained $3e$ worth of electrons and is negatively charged, which is option (a). Nothing was created: the charge was only moved from one object to the other.

exercises.prompt:
In an experiment, a student runs a comb through his hair several times and brings it close to small pieces of paper. Which of the following will he observe?
  1. Pieces of paper repel the comb.
  2. Pieces of paper are attracted to the comb.
  3. Some pieces of paper are attracted and some repel the comb.
  4. There is no attraction or repulsion between the pieces of paper and the comb.

options: Pieces of paper repel the comb.
Pieces of paper are attracted to the comb.
Some pieces of paper are attracted and some repel the comb.
There is no attraction or repulsion between the pieces of paper and the comb.
answer.hint: Running the comb through the hair charges it by rubbing. The pieces of paper are neutral, and a neutral object is drawn toward a charge of either sign.

exercises.prompt:
In an experiment a negatively charged balloon (balloon X) is repelled by another charged balloon Y. However, an object Z is attracted to balloon Y. Which of the following can be the charge on Z? Select two answers.
  1. negative
  2. positive
  3. neutral
  4. cannot be determined

answer.solution: Work out balloon Y first. X is negative and Y repels it, and only like charges repel, so Y is negative too. Now Z is attracted to Y. Unlike charges attract, so Z may be positive, which is option (b). A neutral object is also drawn toward a charge of either sign, as the pieces of paper are drawn toward the comb, so Z may be neutral as well, which is option (c). It cannot be negative, since two negative charges would repel. The two answers are therefore (b) and (c).

exercises.prompt: Suppose an object has a charge of 1 C and gains 6.88×10<sup>18</sup> electrons. (a) What will be the net charge of the object? (b) If the object has gained electrons from a neutral object, what will be the charge on the neutral object? (c) Find and explain the relationship between the total charges of the two objects before and after the transfer. (d) When a third object is brought in contact with the first object (after it gains the electrons), the resulting charge on the third object is 0.4 C. What was its initial charge?

parts.hint: The electrons gained carry a charge of $6.88 \times 10^{18}$ times $-1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C. Add that to the 1 C the object began with.
The second object began neutral and lost exactly the electrons the first gained, so it is left with the opposite of the charge that moved.
Two objects in contact share their total charge, and the total is what it was before they touched.

answer.solution: (a) −0.1 C, (b) 1.1 C, (c) Both charges will be equal to 1 C, law of conservation of charge, (d) 0.9 C

exercises.prompt: The charges on two identical metal spheres (placed in a closed system) are -2.4×10<sup>−17</sup> C and -4.8×10<sup>−17</sup> C. (a) How many electrons will be equivalent to the charge on each sphere? (b) If the two spheres are brought in contact and then separated, find the charge on each sphere. (c) Calculate the number of electrons that would be equivalent to the resulting charge on each sphere.

answer.solution: (a) Divide each charge by the basic charge. The first sphere holds $(2.4 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C})/(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}) = 150$ excess electrons and the second $(4.8 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C})/(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}) = 300$, both negative. (b) The system is closed, so the total charge $-2.4 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C} - 4.8 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C} = -7.2 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C}$ is the same after the contact as before it. The spheres are identical, so they share it equally and each is left with $-3.6 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C}$. (c) That charge is $(3.6 \times 10^{-17}\ \text{C})/(1.60 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}) = 225$ excess electrons on each sphere, which is the 150 and the 300 of part (a) shared out between the two.

exercises.prompt:
In an experiment the following observations are made by a student for four charged objects W, X, Y, and Z:
  • A glass rod rubbed with silk attracts W.
  • W attracts Z but repels X.
  • X attracts Z but repels Y.
  • Y attracts W and Z.
Estimate whether the charges on each of the four objects are positive, negative, or neutral.

answer.solution: W is negative, X is positive, Y is negative, Z is neutral.

exercises.prompt: Common static electricity involves charges ranging from nanocoulombs to microcoulombs. (a) How many electrons are needed to form a charge of $-2.00\ \text{nC}$? (b) How many electrons must be removed from a neutral object to leave a net charge of $0.500\ \mu\text{C}$?

parts.hint: Divide the charge by the basic charge $|\kqe| = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C, remembering that a nanocoulomb is $10^{-9}$ C.
A positive charge is a shortage of electrons, so divide $0.500\ \mu\text{C}$, which is $0.500 \times 10^{-6}$ C, by the same basic charge.

exercises.prompt: To start a car engine, the car battery moves $3.75 \times 10^{21}$ electrons through the starter motor. How many coulombs of charge were moved?

answer.hint: Multiply the number of electrons by the charge each one carries, $-1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C; the sign of the answer says which type of charge moved.
